nodes.description: Reduced or absent melanin in epidermal and hair-follicle melanocytes produces variable hypopigmentation of the skin and hair. In OCA1A there is a complete and lifelong absence of pigment (white hair and skin); in OCA1B, OCA2, OCA3, and OCA4 some pigment accumulates over time, and OCA3 in particular can present with reddish-brown (rufous) coloration. Because melanin acts as a broadband ultraviolet protectant and free-radical scavenger, its loss leaves the skin vulnerable to UV-induced damage and an increased risk of skin cancer, especially squamous cell carcinoma in sun-exposed populations.

nodes.description: The convergence point of the three upstream routes. Melanin is synthesized by melanocytes (skin, hair follicle) and the retinal pigment epithelium within specialized organelles called melanosomes. Whether the lesion is in a melanogenic enzyme (TYR, TYRP1, DCT), in the melanosomal ion transport that sets the pH tyrosinase needs (OCA2, SLC45A2, SLC24A5), or in melanosome biogenesis itself (LRMDA), the result is absent or reduced melanin in melanocytes and the retinal pigment epithelium. OCA1A, with complete tyrosinase deficiency, produces no melanin throughout life, whereas hypomorphic and non-TYR forms permit some pigment accumulation.

evidence.snippet: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of inherited disorders of melanin biosynthesis characterized by a generalized reduction in pigmentation of hair, skin and eyes.

nodes.description: The enzymatic arm of OCA. Tyrosinase (TYR) is the rate-limiting enzyme, converting tyrosine to DOPA and DOPA to dopaquinone, and it requires a neutral melanosomal pH and a copper cofactor to work at all. Two further melanosomal enzymes act downstream in the same pathway: tyrosinase-related protein 1 (TYRP1), which oxidises 5,6-dihydroxyindole-2-carboxylic acid (DHICA) monomers into melanin, and dopachrome tautomerase (DCT, also called tyrosinase-related protein 2). Loss of any of the three removes a step from eumelanin synthesis, and the severity tracks how much residual activity remains: TYR null alleles give lifelong complete absence of pigment, while TYRP1 and DCT variants leave milder hypopigmentation.

nodes.description: The non-enzymatic arm of OCA. Tyrosinase works only at neutral pH, but premelanosomes are acidic; neutralisation at the stage II-to-III transition depends on the combined action of several melanosomal membrane transport proteins. OCA2 mediates a chloride-selective anion conductance and is a positive regulator of pH neutralisation; SLC45A2 is proposed to efflux protons coupled to a sugar substrate; SLC24A5 is a potassium-dependent sodium/calcium exchanger whose subcellular site is still disputed. Losing any of them leaves the melanosome acidic, so tyrosinase is inactive and, in the case of OCA2 and SLC45A2, is also mis-trafficked and retained in the ER/Golgi rather than delivered to the melanosome. The transport activities themselves remain incompletely characterised.

nodes.description: The OCA7 route. LRMDA (formerly C10orf11) is not an enzyme or a transporter: it is recruited to the limiting membrane of the melanosome through active RAB32, where it binds the Commander assembly, and mutations causing OCA7 uncouple that RAB32-Commander binding. Loss of LRMDA disturbs melanosome maturation itself - PMEL processing and the stage I to stage II transition - and lowers melanosomal pH, so pigment output falls without any defect in the melanogenic enzymes. LRMDA localises to melanoblasts and melanocytes in human fetal tissue but was not detected in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

nodes.description: Oral nitisinone, an FDA-approved inhibitor of tyrosine degradation (4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase) used for hereditary tyrosinemia type 1, raises plasma tyrosine and is hypothesized to stabilize residual hypomorphic tyrosinase in OCA1B. In an open-label pilot of 5 adults with OCA1B, nitisinone did not increase iris melanin but produced small significant increases in hair and skin pigmentation. This remains investigational rather than an approved OCA therapy.

nodes.description: Melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium is required for normal postnatal development of the fovea and for correct routing of retinal ganglion cell axons. Reduced RPE and iris melanin in OCA leads to foveal hypoplasia, reduced visual acuity, fundus hypopigmentation, and iris transillumination. Crucially, a melanin defect in the RPE causes abnormal decussation (misrouting) of retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic chiasm, with an excess of fibers crossing to the contralateral side; this produces reduced stereoscopic vision and contributes to strabismus. The precise mechanism by which an RPE pigment defect disrupts development of the adjacent neural retina remains incompletely understood, but foveal differentiation continues for months after birth, offering a potential therapeutic window.
